images.caption: One of the Beaton Panels displayed in the National Museum of Scotland. The carvings, commissioned around the 1530s, are believed to have adorned the Cardinal's private apartments in St. Andrews Castle and been removed by his nephew and captain of the castle, John Beaton of Balfour. They were installed in the dining room of Balfour House near Markinch in Fife. The Museum describes them as "an outstanding example of late Gothic woodwork".
images.alt: One of the Beaton Panels displayed in the National Museum of Scotland. images.caption: Castle at St. Andrews From the internet: "The Castle was the former Bishops' Palace, the residence of the Archbishops of St Andrews. The first castle on this site probably dates from around 1200 - evidence in itself that the office was as much political as religious in medieval times. For example, it was the Archbishop of St Andrews who, in 1306, placed the Scottish Crown upon the head of Robert the Bruce at his coronation at Scone in defiance of Edward I, an act for which the Archbishop was later imprisoned."

images.filename: Countermine at St. Andrews Castle - geograph.org.uk - 948871.jpg
images.caption: Countermine at St. Andrews Castle Not perhaps photogenic but historically interesting. During the siege of 1546-47 the besiegers sunk a mine seeking to gain entry, however the defenders dug a countermine which broke into the mine foiling this attempt. Apparently this is now a very rare example.
